narrative:
Your application was denied because the admissions model estimated that you would have a 56.7 percent chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt—meaning you were more likely to fail than to pass. This risk, not your personal qualities, drove the decision.

The single most important factor was your class standing in your third year. You ranked in the 2nd decile, placing you near the bottom of your class. Accepted students, on average, ranked in the 6th decile, so your performance in the latter half of law school raised a serious concern. The higher your rank, the greater the push toward passing; your rank instead pushed strongly toward failure.

Your LSAT score, by contrast, worked in your favor. At 39, it was slightly above the 37.18 average among accepted students, and this was the second-most influential factor. It nudged the prediction toward passing, showing you have strong aptitude for the exam's reasoning demands. Unfortunately, it wasn't enough to offset your class rank.

The third factor was your undergraduate GPA of 3.10, which fell below the 3.23 average of accepted students. This pushed again toward bar exam failure, reinforcing the concerns from your class standing.

What should you do next? Retake the LSAT to build on your existing strength, and consider enrolling in a part-time or less rigorous program where you can focus on improving your grades. A stronger academic record, combined with your solid LSAT, would substantially improve your chances of admission next time.
